#3633. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3632. Ryan Gosling is Officially Reviving The Flintstones for New Project

Ryan Gosling has been incredibly booked and busy of late. He starred in the lead role in the sci-fi smash hit Project Hail Mary earlier this year. In 2027, he'll travel to the galaxy far, far away in Star Wars: Starfighter. Then in 2028 he'll make his long-awaited MCU debut as Ghost Rider, re-teaming with Starfighter director Shawn Levy. If all that wasn't enough, Gosling has lined up one more unexpected project: The Flintstones.

Gosling's production company, Open Invite, and Warner Bros. are in early development on a live-action Flintstones reboot centered on a grown-up Bamm-Bamm, according to Deadline. Currently, Gosling and his Open Invite partner Jessie Henderson are looking for a writer to take on the project. Later this year Open Invite will premiere the romantic drama Love of Your Life at the Toronto International Film Festival. The movie stars Margaret Qualley (The Dog Stars), Aaron Pierre (Lanterns), and Patrick Schwarzenegger (The White Lotus), among others.

Bamm-Bamm first appeared as a baby in the original 1960s Hanna-Barbera cartoon, as the young son of Barney and Betty Rubble. He was depicted as a teenager in The Pebbles and Bamm-Bamm Show in the 1970s, when he started a band with his sister Pebbles. Bamm-Bamm also appeared in the 1994 live-action Flintstones movie.

As Gosling's project is currently in early development, there is no news about who may play Bamm-Bamm or what the story will be. The big question is whether Gosling will be involved in the project beyond his role as a producer. After his widely acclaimed performance as Ken in Greta Gerwig's Barbie, it seems like the actor would be a perfect fit for Bamm-Bamm. Of course, with his schedule already so busy, he may not want to take on yet another project.

There is also the possibility of a Barbie sequel. Warner Bros. would likely prioritize Gosling's return to Barbie over the Flintstones project, since the former is the studio's highest-grossing film.

#3631. Godzilla Minus Zero's Surprise Villain And Its Franchise History Explained

This article contains major spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

The King of the Monsters is back, and this time, he's not alone. Director Takashi Yamazaki has returned with a follow-up to his Oscar-winning smash hit "Godzilla Minus One" in the form of "Godzilla Minus Zero." Topping the film's predecessor was never going to be easy, but Yamazaki brought a not-so-secret weapon: King Ghidorah.

The King Ghidorah design for "Godzilla Minus Zero" leaked online thanks to merchandise, despite Toho trying to keep the monster's reveal a secret from the viewing public. But now, the cat is out of the bag, and this movie winds up being a showdown between Godzilla and one of his oldest foes. And much in the same way that Yamazaki reinvented Godzilla in "Minus One," he very much puts his own stamp on Ghidorah in "Minus Zero."

Anyone who has seen the sequel undoubtedly knows that King Ghidorah is a wildly powerful, foreboding kaiju. The design of the monster is very faithful to what fans of the franchise have known for years, but he's also modernized with some terrifying additions, including some wild new abilities that lead to some downright jaw-dropping action sequences. "Godzilla Minus Zero" is rated R, and that allows Yamazaki to not hold back in terms of the destruction and chaos caused by this hulking beast.

As even casual "Godzilla" fans are surely aware, this is far from the first time that Ghidorah has gone toe-to-toe with the King himself. So, in light of his latest appearance, it's worth looking back at the monster's history, how he's evolved over the years, and how this movie puts a new twist on him.

King Ghidorah first appeared on-screen in 1964's "Ghidorah, the "Three-Headed Monster," one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time. By that point, the "Godzilla" franchise had become rather popular, and the titular monster was no longer alone. He'd faced off against Anguirus, King Kong, and Mothra. So, Ghidorah was far from the first kaiju battle for Godzilla, but he set a new high bar and instantly asserted himself as Godzilla's most powerful foe.

In terms of his origins, King Ghidorah is an alien monster who wiped out an alien race on Venus and came to Earth on a meteor. Ghidorah was such a formidable threat that the only way he could be defeated was to unite Godzilla, Mothra, and Rodan together against him. Ghidorah is truly one of the only monsters that might be scarier than Godzilla. This was essentially the first time that Godzilla went from villain to humanity's savior (although that line was already starting to blur by then).

Ghidorah quickly became a staple of the property. He re-appeared a year later in 1965's "Invasion of the Astro-Monster" and then again in 1968's "Destroy All Monsters," which features one of the most iconic "Godzilla" movie moments (Ghidorah getting stomped out by a group of kaiju). Ghidorah has since come back for every era of the franchise, including 1991's "Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah" during the Heisei era (which also introduced Mecha-King Ghidorah).

He later appeared in the Millennium era in 2001's chaotic "Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack" and in the MonsterVerse in 2019's "Godzilla: King of the Monsters." Rivaled perhaps only by Mothra, Ghidorah truly is Godzilla's most notorious foe. And where Mothra is often an ally, Ghidorah is as bad as they come.

On the one hand, Takashi Yamazaki is very faithful to King Ghidorah in "Godzilla Minus Zero." At the same time, though, he makes the monster feel fresh again with a terrifying makeover, one that fits in very well with the universe he set up in "Minus One." Ghidorah still shoots lightning bolts from his mouth, has that gold, scaly skin and those three dangerous heads, and remains massive. But there's an evolution to the kaiju here that makes this version particularly terrifying.

The very first scene of the movie shows us Ghidorah in a new form, namely what looks, for all intents and purposes, like a dragon with just one head. His design would be right at home in "Reign of Fire" (one of many fantasy movies that didn't deserve to flop at the box office). But I digress. After this initial attack, we learn that Ghidorah arrived on Earth via a meteor, keeping his alien origins intact.

Yamazaki's big change comes when Japan tries to kill a dormant Ghidorah. After dropping a bomb on him and impaling him so that he'll be struck with lightning, Ghidorah evolves into his final, more familiar form. The biggest change is his horrifying ability to use gravity beams, literally lifting towns into the sky and dropping them down to Earth.

The big climax relies on the film's humans forcing Godzilla to fight Ghidorah in a winner-take-all grudge match. Godzilla wins by blowing Ghidorah to pieces, but it isn't easy. The ending of "Godzilla Minus Zero" doesn't make it clear where the franchise goes from here, but it does leave some doors open. However, what isn't left dangling is any question as to who reigns supreme. At the end of the day, Godzilla is still the king.

#3630. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

#3629. Godzilla Minus Zero Finally Explains How Noriko Survived Minus One

This article contains spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

One of the most anticipated sequels of the year is finally upon us. "Godzilla Minus Zero" is the follow-up to 2024's "Godzilla Minus One," with director Takashi Yamazaki returning to once again put his stamp on the legendary franchise. And since "Godzilla Minus One" was officially the first movie in the franchise to win an Oscar, the pressure is on.

Thus far, the first reactions to "Godzilla Minus Zero" have been glowing, so it's fair to say mission accomplished. A big reason for that is because Yamazaki picked up where he left off, centering the action on the same characters two years later as Japan attempts to dig itself out of the devastation left behind by Godzilla's attacks. Specifically, Ryûnosuke Kamiki is back as Kōichi Shikishima and Minami Hamabe is back as Noriko as they both try to build a life for their adopted daughter, Akiko (Sae Nagatani).

As viewers will surely recall, Noriko was left for dead after Godzilla annihilated the Ginza District in "Minus One," which is one of the worst things that Godzilla has ever done. Miraculously and somewhat inexplicably, Noriko survived the attack. Shikishima and Akiko reunited with her in the hospital at the very end of the movie, and all seemed well — or mostly well, anyway. Noriko had a very strange, scaly growth on her neck, implying that something was amiss.

One of the biggest questions viewers were left with was how in the heck Norkiko survived Godzilla's devastating blast. It seemed like it was just for the sake of giving the movie a happy ending. However, "Minus Zero" not only explains how Noriko survived, but uses that as a major plot device that the sequel hinges on.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" shows the horrifying aftermath of a kaiju attack like never before, revisiting key events from "Minus One" from new perspectives. One of these scenes explains how Noriko survived. We meet Dr. Ogata (Jun Kunimura), who treated Noriko after the attacks in 1947. He explains that there's no way this woman should have survived. She was on death's door — so much so that he told a nurse to leave her and tend to someone else.

Miraculously, the following day, she was breathing with a strong heartbeat. Within days of that, her wounds had all but disappeared, save for her eye. The explanation? Godzilla's G cells were infused into several survivors. These cells have regenerative properties, which explains why Noriko's terrible wounds healed. Unfortunately, it's not all good news.

Every other person who was infected with the G cells died, with scaly growths emerging from their skin. This explains the markings on Noriko's neck at the end of "Minus One." But she was also the only one who managed to live this long with the G cells in her body. Those G cells are later used to help lure Godzilla to the final battle with King Ghidorah, using Dr. Murakami's amplification device. Throughout the movie, Noriko says she doesn't have much time left, as the scaly growths continue to spread.

In retrospect, it's interesting that the happy ending in "Godzilla Minus One" almost didn't happen. That ending teed up much of the sequel's plot and some of the more harrowing scenes in the franchise. Whether or not Noriko survives much longer is an open-ended question, but at the very least, Takashi Yamazaki didn't merely save her for the sake of putting a nice bow on the previous movie. There was a meaningful, in-universe explanation for that decision.

#3627. GTA 6's Biggest Competition Officially Arrives on PC in 2027

NetEase is trying to make the everything game with Ananta

Grand Theft Auto 6 is set to dominate 2026 with its long-awaited release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, another game — one heavily inspired by GTA, Marvel's Spider-Man, and Genshin Impact — will give Rockstar Games a run for its money: Ananta.

NetEase games showed up at Gamescom Opening Night Live in a big way this summer with Ananta. The game, which is basically "anime Grand Theft Auto," has been buzzy ever since it was announced, and now we have an official release date in early 2027.

Ananta's release date trailer begins with a short setup of the game's story, which seems pretty light. Players will take on the role of a supernatural investigator tasked with battling some evil guys. It doesn't seem all that important, but seeing the protagonist hang off the side of a plane mid-flight like he's Tom Cruise is admittedly pretty cool. Then we got a look at more gameplay that leans into the Grand Theft Auto comparisons. You'll explore two sprawling open-world cities and drive or fly around in scooters, cars, and more futuristic-looking vehicles. It will also include plenty of mini-games and activities to get invested in outside the main story.

Not to be outdone by Grand Theft Auto 6's release, Ananta offers more than familiar riffs on Rockstar's series. Previous trailers have shown that NetEase is taking inspiration from almost every AAA game under the sun. That includes the ability to swing across the game's gorgeous anime cities like you are Spider-Man. It really seems like NetEase is pumping as much money as possible into Ananta and striving to deliver a true "everything" game that has something for every gamer out there.

While Ananta will be free-to-play, it does not seem to be a gacha game in the vein of Genshin Impact and Honkai: Star Rail. There will be in-game purchases, but they'll be focused on cosmetics, vehicles, and other decorations rather than character unlocks. In that sense, it seems like Ananta will be a social RPG competing most with Grand Theft Auto Online.

Ananta will be released on Jan. 15, 2027 on PlayStation 5 and Windows PC, with mobile versions for Android and iOS.

#3626. The 11 Best Video Game Remakes of All Time, Ranked

The act of remixing and remaking a previously beloved work of art has been pervasive in all different mediums and forms of entertainment, yet there are distinct elements of video games as a medium that make their respective remakes different from other art forms. While movie and television remakes are often defined by their change in artistic vision and technological improvements, video game remakes often take the initiative of refining poorly aged aspects of the original games, making use of the exponential growth of technical capabilities, or just simply making the game readily available to modern gamers.

This has resulted in many video game remakes, when they are successful, not only living up to the stature and legacy of the original games, but in many ways replacing the original in terms of replayability, being the definitive ways to experience these legendary titles. Remakes come in all different forms and approaches, but the very best video game remakes find this perfect balance between delivering the strengths of the original game and having something new and exciting to offer.

Paper Mario: The Thousand Year Door continues to be celebrated as one of the very best games on the GameCube, with its overwhelming charm and engaging battle system making it the fan-favorite peak of the Paper Mario franchise. However, the series largely abandoned the signature battle system and engrossing worldbuilding that made the game such a hit, making it all the more exciting that the game was receiving a super polished remake in the modern age.

It would be great enough to simply release the exact same masterpiece for modern consoles, but the Nintendo Switch remake of Paper Mario: The Thousand-Year Door adds just enough quality of life changes to make it the definitive version of the game. Most notably, the game makes improvements to pacing through the addition of a fast travel area and a quicker way to switch between partners. The game also features two new secret bosses to challenge veterans of the original game and a better translation of the original Japanese version of the game, portraying fan-favorite character Vivian as a transgender woman.

The game just came out, so it's still early to tell how much of a legacy and impact this will have on the larger gaming industry as a whole, but the beautifully constructed Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time flourishes and evolves what was already one of the greatest games of all time. With beautiful visuals, a multitude of quality-of-life changes, and full voice acting, this remake is the complete package and a love letter to one of Nintendo's most cherished gaming experiences.

As influential as the original game was and as great as it still is to this day, this remake serves to solve and update the game to the modern standards of not just visuals, but primarily control and ease of access in experiencing its mastery. The remake leaves a mark on gamers who experience it, whether they've played through the original game constantly since it was released or they only just recently got into the series with games like Breath of the Wild.

Following in the footsteps of the other major horror video game franchise's tendency to create massive, fully-fledged remakes of their most beloved classic titles, it was only a matter of time before Silent Hill 2 was given the AAA remake treatment. While the series as a whole has had a middling reception and was outright abandoned for large chunks of the 2010s, there was a lot of clear passion and care put into this remake to make it faithful to the original masterpiece as possible.

The major strength of this remake is to provide a modern third-person camera system and a more dynamic combat system to a central narrative that is still celebrated as one of the very best in video game history. All of the strengths of its story and emotional beats are still there, with even legendary composer Akira Yamaoka returning to remix his all-time classic themes. It certainly helped that the game was largely developed by Bloober Team, a dev team of deeply passionate horror game fans who were inspired by the original Silent Hill 2 in the first place.

Yakuza had always been an appreciated franchise, but it reached an overwhelming state of newfound success and appreciation following the release of series prequel Yakuza 0, putting the series in the perfect spot for a high-profile remake of the first game in the series. Yakuza Kiwami makes use of a lot of the improvements that the series has made since its humble PS2 beginnings, more directly honing into its distinct voice for hard-hitting crime drama as well as wildly goofy and over-the-top comedic side content.

It also helps that this remake more directly amplifies some of the most celebrated aspects of the entire series, having some of the most iconic side missions and a perfect portrayal of the iconic rivalry between Kazuma Kiryu and Goro Majima. This game has outright replaced the status of the original game in the eyes of many Yakuza fans, as well as being one of the best entry points to the franchise in all of its brilliance.

While video game remakes directly utilizing the improvements of technological advancements largely seems like a modern trend, this phenomenon has been occurring even during the 16-bit era of gaming, with one of the best examples being Super Castlevania IV. The SNES classic acts as a remake of the original NES classic, seeing Simon Belmont facing off against the monsters in Dracula's castle looking to defeat the infamous monster.

The game is a perfect example of just how much video games as a medium was growing and evolving in the 80s and 90s, having massive visual and gameplay improvements despite releasing only 5 years after the original game. It adds more exciting gameplay elements, increases the scale and memorability of its missions, and features one of the absolute best video game soundtracks of all time. The game is still considered one of the best games in the franchise and one of the best games on the SNES.

Four worlds and four completely different ideas of what a good life looks like. This is where you belong, what it would ask of you, and what you would get back in return.

You belong somewhere old enough that the mountains have names and somebody can still tell you who gave them. Middle-earth is for people who think the right thing is worth doing even when it will not be finished in their lifetime.

You want the sea, a crew, and absolutely nobody telling you where you are allowed to go. The Grand Line is the world for people whose main ambition in life is finding out what is over there.

You would rather be feared and useful than liked and useless. The Continent is a world where the monsters are the straightforward part of the job and the people are where it all gets complicated.

You want the myths to be real and loose in the actual world, and you want to find out at about thirteen that you were never anywhere near as ordinary as everybody kept telling you.

The Persona series was already massively celebrated and acclaimed when Persona 3 first released, but the series saw a massive explosion in popularity and visual style following the overwhelming success of Persona 5. This largely led to the creation of Persona 3 Reload, which acted as a definitive modern remake of the classic PS2 game that utilized the visual flair and brilliance of Persona 5. Reload proves to be incredibly faithful to the storytelling and character of the original game while upgrading it to the modern standards of the series.

In terms of pure polish, the game is one of the most beautiful and striking pieces of visual art that gaming currently has to offer, elevating and evolving what was already a game with half-decent visuals into a masterclass of style. While the visuals are the clear immediate strength of this remake, the game also makes a lot of quality of life changes to better align its gameplay with the systems of Persona 5. It overall just makes for a more impactful and compelling version of what was already one of the best JRPGs ever made.

The original Shadow of the Colossus was one of the most critically acclaimed adventure games of its era, with its beautiful and somber tone mixed with the massive scale of its boss fights making it a true work of art that pushed the medium forward. Considering just how much of the original game was defined by its then pristine graphics and the weight of its scale, amplifying and further iterating on this scale in a full 4K remake for PS4 made the Shadow of the Colossus remake an undeniable leap forward.

Development team Bluepoint Games already had experience in recreating the strengths of Shadow of the Colossus, having previously developed the PS3 remaster of the game. However, this remake proves to be a massive leap forward in terms of the visual brilliance and scale of the game, making its most iconic moments all the more breathtaking and captivating for players to experience.

Many of the games from the 8-bit era of gaming, as massively influential and important as they were for the industry as a whole, certainly don't hold up nearly as well when placed under a modern lens. In terms of actively updating and evolving one of these legendary titles to fit the standard of its modern titles, Metroid: Zero Mission is about as great as a remake of an 8-bit game can get. This Game Boy Advance classic and remake of the NES original Metroid adds so much new content to the original classic that it's almost staggering.

It's filled with new puzzles, more engaging combat, and a whole slew of new bosses and areas that expand upon the world and story of the NES original. While the original Metroid continues to be defined by its age, Zero Mission is one of the most timeless and well-crafted entries in the entire franchise, to many people being one of the high-points of the franchise in terms of its 2D entries.

Few video game franchises have been as consistent and frequent with their updated remakes of classic titles as the Pokémon series, as their remakes often go beyond simply porting the original game, but create vast, new experiences complete with all sorts of content and changes from the modern games. While several Pokémon remakes have surpassed their original games in the eyes of fans, Pokémon HeartGold and SoulSilver were so beautifully crafted in their recreation of the Generation 2 games that they are still considered some of the best Pokémon games ever made.

HeartGold and Soulsilver are not just defined by how effectively they match the original games, but also by just how much new content and experiences that they add to this title. Gameplay additions that have been added since the Game Boy Color days, like Abilities and the Physical Special split, made an overwhelming difference in terms of the feel of the game and Pokemon battling as a whole. The game also has the fan-favorite feature of having Pokemon follow the player around, a feature many fans still beg to be included in modern games to this day.

It's a lofty undertaking to remake and modernize one of the most influential video games of all time, even moreso, that Final Fantasy VII would end up being remade not just in the form of one game, but an entire trilogy of AAA experiences. While the trilogy itself is set to conclude this upcoming April with Final Fantasy VII Revelation, the highlight of this trilogy still stands as the iconic first game, Final Fantasy VII Remake. The essential PS5 game expands and builds upon the first act of the original game, creating a complete action RPG experience from the iconic locale of Midgar.

It speaks volumes that Final Fantasy VII Remake is adapting what is only the first 7–10 hours of the original PS1 game and transforming it into a fully complete, nearly 100-hour adventure complete with engaging fights, emotional storybeats, and a dynamic remix of its classic story. The game further redefines what a Final Fantasy game can be in the modern age of gaming while staying true to the brilliance and timelessness of the original game.

#3625. Godzilla Minus Zero's King Ghidorah Has One Scene That Was 55 Years In The Making

This article contains minor spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is here, with director Takashi Yamazaki once again getting to put his stamp on the King of the Monsters. He also got to offer up his take on another classic kaiju this time around in the form of King Ghidorah. The monster's appearance was a poorly kept secret, with Ghidorah's design in "Godzilla Minus Zero" leaking thanks to merchandise. But in any event, the monster's inclusion helped resolve a 55-year-old dream for the filmmaker.

According to Reuters, Yamazaki grew up in the Japanese ‌city of Matsumoto. A big "Godzilla" fan, he was particularly excited about 1964's "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time. In particular, he hoped to see the kaiju wreck shop in his hometown. Unfortunately, Matsumoto only appeared fleetingly in the movie after Ghidorah's emergence.

Given that "Godzilla Minus One" became the highest-grossing Japanese Godzilla movie ever en route to winning an Oscar, Yamazaki was given a lot of creative freedom on the sequel. He used that freedom to show Ghidorah doing what he wanted to see as a child. "Minus Zero" prominently features Matsumoto, with Ghidorah carving a path of destruction there relatively early on in the movie's runtime. Here's what the filmmaker had to say about it:

"55 years later, I had King ‌Ghidorah ​appear in my own film. I had the chance ⁠to make the movie I ⁠wanted to watch back then, and I created the footage that I wanted to show my younger self, as if to say, 'This is what you wanted to see, isn't it?'"

"So, my dream has finally come true after ​55 years, and I am truly happy," Takashi Yamazaki concluded.

The sequel picks up two years after the events of "Minus One" as Japan is still trying to put itself back together in the aftermath of Godzilla's attacks. Things are once again thrown into chaos when a new, mysterious, dragon-like monster emerges. It's not long before Godzilla is back as well, leaving the people of Japan scrambling to figure out how to deal with not one but two kaiju.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is rated R, which meant that Yamazaki didn't have to hold back at all. When it came to having King Ghidorah destroy his hometown, he certainly made the most of that R rating. In a bizarre method of showing pride for the place he came from, he made the most of Matsumoto in his latest cinematic effort. Being from Japan and having your home shown off in a "Godzilla" movie is, understandably, something to be proud of.

King Ghidorah was the movie's "surprise" villain who has a long history with the franchise. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was his first of many, many appearances across the many eras of this franchise. In recent years, he's been showcased in everything from "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" in the MonsterVerse to the animated "Godzilla: The Planet Eater" on Netflix. He's without a doubt Godzilla's most notorious foe.

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3624. These Surprisingly Powerful Soundcore Earbuds Are Under $35 Right Now

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

The Soundcore P31i earbuds are down to $32.99 (originally $59.99), which is as low as they’ve been, according to price trackers. At this price, most earbuds stick to the basics, so it’s unusual to see features like active noise cancellation and LDAC included here. That doesn’t mean they compete with premium pairs, but they do give you more to work with than you’d expect for under $35.

These earbuds are light, they fit well, and they don’t get uncomfortable after an hour or two, which isn’t always the case with cheaper earbuds. Battery life, too, holds up through a full day of use, with a little over seven hours on a single charge and extra top-ups from the case. The sound quality is better than expected for the price, though it leans toward bass-heavy tuning out of the box (you can tweak it in the app, but the app itself is not the most intuitive and takes some getting used to, notes this ZDNET review), and if you’re using a compatible device, LDAC support gives you the option for better audio quality.

There are also a few extras tucked in, like HearID for tuning the sound to your ears and an AI translation feature, though features like that feel more like a bonus than something you will use every day. As for its noise cancellation, it works, but expectations need to stay in check—it reduces steady background noise like engines and traffic, but it won’t match the isolation you get from more expensive earbuds. That lines up with its overall build, as well, which feels a bit basic compared to more expensive options.

#3623. 5 Best New Movies And Shows To Stream This Weekend On Netflix, Apple TV, Hulu, And More (Nov. 6-8)

It's the first full weekend of November, the weather is finally turning truly chilly, and Halloweekend is in the rear-view mirror. Whether you went all-out on your costume last weekend or you elected to slap a nametag with a different moniker on your shirt and call it a day (which is my preferred way to celebrate Halloween if asked to do so), this weekend is perfect for staying in and curling up with a fresh series or movie. So, what's new on the big streamers?

Between Apple, Peacock, Hulu, and Netflix, there's a decent spate of new releases heading to streaming this weekend (and some of them even dropped earlier in the week). Whether you want to watch a gripping spy drama, a truly ridiculous legal drama, a breezy sports comedy, a crime thriller tinged with romance, or a quick-paced series featuring one of the best and weirdest pairings in TV history, I've got you covered.

Director Adam Carter Rehmeier, known for indie films like "Snack Shack" and "Dinner in America," teamed up with modern scream queen Samara Weaving and horror staple Kyle Gallner for this year's "Carolina Caroline" — which just hit Netflix, marking its first home on a major streaming service. Weaving, who also led "Ready or Not 2: Here I Come" and "Over Your Dead Body" recently (and who's joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe to play Emma Frost), stars as Caroline Daniels, a gas station attendant who falls in love with Gallner's con artist Oliver Anderson. As the two make their way to South Carolina from rural Texas, they end up committing robbery after robbery, leaving destruction in their wake.

Weaving's Caroline and Gallner's Oliver make for a great modern Bonnie and Clyde, and "Carolina Caroline" is a gripping, entertaining, and extraordinarily fun film that also features Jon Gries ("Napoleon Dynamite," "The White Lotus") and Kyra Sedgwick in supporting roles. If you want a crime drama packed with plenty of romance, "Carolina Caroline" on Netflix is your best bet.

Congratulations to all bad TV enjoyers: One of the worst shows ever made is back for Season 2! Ryan Murphy's gleefully ludicrous legal drama "All's Fair," which undoubtedly gives real lawyers raging headaches if they dare to tune in, stars Kim Kardashian as high-powered lawyer Allura Grant, who works alongside Liberty Ronson (Naomi Watts), Emerald J. Greene-Ball (Niecy Nash-Betts), Dina Standish (Glenn Close), and Milan (Teyana Taylor) at a firm that handles divorces. Sarah Paulson, a regular Murphy collaborator, livens up proceedings as rival lawyer Carrington "Carr" Lane, who is unbelievably twisted and extremely fun, and Nash-Betts, Watts, and Close are all game to ham it up.

I don't think I'm blowing anyone's mind when I say Kim Kardashian is a generationally dreadful actor who should not even appear in commercials, let alone a scripted drama that could be dishy and fun if she wasn't swanning around with absolutely zero expression in every single scene. Still, if you dig wildly bad TV and just want to switch your brain off, check out "All's Fair." Besides, if nothing else, it has given us an incredible episode of its fellow Hulu series "The Kardashians" where Close, out of character, gets very drunk off martinis at Kris Jenner's house.

I love "30 Rock," I have immense respect for weird little guy and short king Daniel Radcliffe, and I've been riding for Bobby Moynihan since the first time I saw him perform as Drunk Uncle on "Saturday Night Live." Essentially, "The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins" — which stars Tracy Morgan, was created by Robert Carlock and Sam Means, is executive produced by Tina Fey, and stars Morgan and Radcliffe as the unlikeliest and best duo in recent TV memory — was made for me in a lab. My enduring affection for this show aside, I think it's sure to delight pretty much anybody, and when Season 1 premiered in January, it immediately became one of the best shows of 2026.

The premise? Morgan plays Reggie Dinkins, a disgraced NFL star who was banned from the New York Jets and all other professional teams in the league after being caught betting on his games. (Hilariously, he only bet on his own performance to inspire himself to play better.) Thus, Reggie tries to regain his tattered reputation alongside his best friend and former teammate Rusty (Moynihan), his ex-wife and manager Monica (Erika Alexander), his young but extremely compatible fiancée Brina (Precious Joy), his son Carmelo (Jalyn Hall), and Radcliffe's Oscar-winning documentarian Arthur Tobin. With Arthur living in his palatial suburban New York mansion to make a documentary that will hopefully relaunch Reggie's career and get him into the NFL Hall of Fame, Reggie does his best to refurbish his image, and the results are extremely funny. "Reggie Dinkins" Season 2 dropped on NBC and Peacock on November 2, and if you're returning to this near-perfect series, welcome back. If you're new, go laugh your way through Season 1, then join us.

If you enjoyed Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw's delightful spy drama "Black Doves" when it dropped back on Netflix in 2024, you'll be pleased to hear the series — created by Joe Barton — released its second season on the streamer on November 5. Across six episodes, we pick up where the show left off with Helen Dawson (Knightley), a secret Black Doves operative who sells secrets to the highest bidder and also happens to be married to a Conservative MP for a major UK constituency and Secretary of State for Defense, Wallace Webb (Andrew Buchan). In the beginning of Season 1, Helen is shocked and saddened to learn that her lover, Jason Davies (Andre Koji), has died under suspicious circumstances ... and her secret identity may now be at risk.

Throughout that first season, Helen teams up with her old friend and hired assassin Sam Young (Whishaw), who's sent by the Doves to help protect her. In Season 2, after a shocking cliffhanger ending, we follow Helen and Sam as he desperately tries to keep her safe, even as she's targeted by nefarious forces throughout England. Knightley and Whishaw are fantastic together, and if you sort of forgot "Black Doves" was a thing since Season 1 premiered 2 years ago, I'm happy to tell you that it's back and still an extremely fun and enthralling watch.

Apple TV has some of the best comedy series on television hiding on its service (which seems to get overlooked in favor of ones like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime Video), and if you're a fan of "Ted Lasso" but haven't watched "Stick," you're really missing out. Owen Wilson leads this sports comedy created by Jason Keller and stars as Pryce Cahill, a former golf pro nicknamed "The Stick" who's stuck selling clubs and coaching at a country club after years of a career decline. At work one day, Pryce meets a gifted young golfer, Santi Wheeler (Peter Dager), who quit golfing after some personal issues got in the way of his game. Determined to make Santi the next golf star, Pryce ends up roping him into a cross-country tour to show off his talents alongside Santi's mother Elena (Mariana Treviño), Pryce's former caddy Mitts (Marc Maron), and a onetime bartender and current caddy Zero Duffy (Lili Kay), all of whom pile into an RV to make the trip.

"Stick" Season 2 adds great actors like Timothy Olyphant (as Pryce's former golf rival Clark Ross) as regulars and guest stars like recent Emmy winner Rhea Seehorn as Pryce's former coach, with Billy Zane also joining Season 2 in an as-yet-unknown capacity. The first two episodes of the sophomore season dropped on November 4, so catch up before it continues its run.

#3622. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

#3621. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

#3620. 10 Devastating Game Cancellations That Are Still Disappointing Years Later

The best games ever — from an alternate timeline

Sometimes, it’s fun to think about the great games that might have been — until they were canceled without ever getting the chance to make their mark. Most of the time, we just shrug our shoulders and move on, because that’s life. But sometimes, we mourn the wasted potential.

Some of those canceled games might have fought the odds and disappointed us anyway, like Duke Nukem Forever. Others might just as easily have become massive hits, if only they had been allocated additional time and resources. In that regard, they’re a bit like Schrodinger’s cat. With both possible outcomes in mind, here are the 10 canceled games we’re still upset about years later. They could have been contenders!

Players looking forward to a shooter set in the StarCraft universe had twelve years to hope and dream before finally having to accept that nothing was ever going to come of StarCraft: Ghost. First announced in 2002, the title spent several years in active development before being placed on indefinite hold in 2006. Over the course of those years, the industry changed a lot. For that matter, so did the development team. Although there has been a lot of discussion about what went wrong with StarCraft: Ghost, the game’s eventual cancellation was due to numerous factors. Perhaps the biggest of them was the success of a different Blizzard property: World of Warcraft. We can easily understand why Blizzard management would have chosen to allocate resources toward a property that was red-hot at the time. Even so, it stings a little that StarCraft didn’t get its spinoff.

Electronic Arts, who would have been the one to publish Dead Space 4, technically never announced it. Years later, we only know the game was in development because some of the developers responsible have said so. Originally, it began development in February of 2013, following the launch of Dead Space 3. That previous game clearly didn’t sell as well as Electronic Arts hoped. Since the writing was on the wall, leadership chose to have Visceral focus on other projects. Dead Space 4 development ended not long after it began, and well before any playable levels could be built. The development studio itself followed in 2017. As for the franchise, it seems to be done for, especially after the terrific Dead Space remake failed to expand its audience.

History has proven that games can be all but finished and still get canceled. Such was the case for Fable Legends, a multiplayer action-RPG that was preparing for its open beta phase at the time of its cancellation in 2016. First revealed at Gamescom in 2013, the game spent around four years in development. Developer Lionhead Studios had just finished Fable Journey and said goodbye to co-founder Peter Molyneux when it went to work on a new action-RPG intended to showcase the power of the Xbox One. A live service game might not seem like the right fit for a studio known for its single-player prowess, but Microsoft executives knew best and they were willing to spend piles of money to make their vision a reality. When the game’s development finally ended in 2016, just shy of a proper release, so did Lionhead Studios.

The California Raisins: The Grape Escape came about as close to releasing as a game can without entering the manufacturing process, then dropped out of sight at the last minute. If you read old gaming magazines, you’ll sometimes find pictures of the familiar dried fruit mascot in sunglasses, forcing its way around a plump bunch of grapes. But the ads and all references to the game disappeared overnight. One possible reason for the abrupt change is the fact that the raisins and their crooning style were already on their way out of fashion. Capcom also had other big projects to tend to. For context, 1990 is the same year it released Mega Man 3 and Gargoyle’s Quest in North America, along with numerous arcade titles. Besides that, the Super Nintendo was fast approaching. But at least for fans of the raisins, there’s good news: someone found a prototype cart and dumped its contents all over the internet. If you want to see what the game was all about, you technically can, even though it never got its flowers.

In 2006, we learned that we could look forward to playing Star Wars Battlefront 3, this time from Free Radical Design instead of Pandemic Studios. Then in late 2008, we learned that we shouldn’t look forward to it at all when LucasArts canceled the project. During the time it spent on the game, the team reportedly produced a build that was nearly final. Unfortunately, Free Radical Design and LucasArts couldn’t reach an agreement to carry that third installment across the finish line and serve it up to players. Then, in 2016, an Xbox 360 prototype leaked. It provided a glimpse of how the game might have played, had it been released. Next, a fully playable Wii build of Star Wars Battlefront 3 materialized in late 2024. We finally got to see what we had missed. Sadly, nothing could give us back the 16 years we had to live without that experience.

Game engines are supposed to simplify the development process, but they don’t always achieve that result. Unreal Engine 4 enabled some amazing games to come to fruition, but it didn’t streamline things for the team at PlatinumGames, which wrestled with the engine and ultimately failed to deliver Scalebound to Microsoft. First announced at E3 in 2014, the promising game was scheduled to arrive in 2016. Then it slipped into the next year and finally was canceled when the developer failed to produce a stable, playable piece of software. Perhaps the ambitious team, led by Hideki Kamiya of Bayonetta fame, simply tried to do more than its resources permitted. Maybe there were other less interesting problems. Whatever the case, the game never happened and probably never will. That’s a shame. The story of a boy and his dragon is one we would have liked to see.

There must be something about Star Wars, because two games from that franchise found their way to this list. Star Wars 1313 was to be an action-adventure game focusing on everyone’s favorite bounty hunter, Boba Fett. Handled internally at LucasArts, the title spent roughly three years in development. When Disney acquired LucasArts in late 2012, there was still a ways to go. Unfortunately, the new owners weren’t interested in paying to provide the necessary runway, especially not after investing more than $4 billion to buy the company. They canceled the project around six months later, leaving us to mourn what might have been. The closest we’ll probably ever get to a Star Wars experience along similar lines is Ubisoft’s semi-recent release, Star Wars Outlaws.

Some publishers consider sales in excess of 1 million units a success, but Square Enix is not one of them. At least, it wasn’t when the title in question was Sleeping Dogs (previously set to be published by Activision as True Crime: Hong Kong). It presented an engaging environment that compared favorably to the likes of Ubisoft’s Watch Dogs, but it failed to meet sales projections. United Front Games then went to work on a sequel that would have expanded the story and offered two-player cooperative play, among other enhancements. Square Enix passed on the pitch, however, and encouraged the team to build the project that became Triad Wars… which only made it as far as a beta phase before it also got shut down. For United Front Games and the Sleeping Dogs franchise both, that cancellation marked the end of the line.

If you own a working PlayStation 4 with the demo of Silent Hills (originally known as P.T.) installed, you have a piece of history. First revealed in August 2014 as a playable teaser, the game’s development united Hideo Kojima (best known for Metal Gear Solid) and Hollywood horror director Guillermo del Toro. The happy pair planned to work with actor Norman Reedus to revitalize the popular Silent Hill horror franchise, which had fallen upon hard times. Eight months later, Konami canceled the game-in-progress and Kojima left the company to make Death Stranding (partnering with Reedus again). A few years later, Capcom presented a fresh take on Resident Evil with a seventh installment that reminded some players of P.T. As for Konami, it wasn’t done with Silent Hill. In fact, Silent Hill: Townfall, a promising new installment from No Code and Annapurna Interactive, is due next month.

Capcom didn’t quite have a massive hit with its two Mega Man Legends games (three if you count The Misadventures of Tron Bonne). Still, it had cultivated an audience that it decided to pursue with a third numbered installment. Announced as an early 3DS title in September 2010, Mega Man Legends 3 incorporated feedback from a community of Mega Man fans. Eager players voted on characters, designs, and mechanics as development progressed. When Capcom canceled the project in July of 2011, not long after Keiji Inafune left the company in late 2010, the move felt very abrupt. A demo was on its way, with multiple levels and a new protagonist, but it never got released. The 3DS recovered from its alarming weak launch and went on to become a genuinely successful platform, but the reversal of fortune came too late to spare the third installment in Capcom’s niche series. Its cancellation means the cliffhanger at the end of Mega Man Legends 2 remains unresolved to this day. Maybe Capcom will come back to the series in the future to explore what comes next, but we wouldn’t count on it. In the meantime, at least we have Mega Man: Dual Override to look forward to in 2027.

#3619. How Big Godzilla Is In Godzilla Minus One Compared To Other Movie Sizes

Godzilla Minus Zero is finally here, and here is how big Godzilla is in the film compared to how tall he is in other Godzilla movies. One of Godzilla's most iconic trademarks is his size, with the terrifying titular titan towering over cities as he brings them to rubble. Tons of iterations of Godzilla have been presented throughout cinema history, with the different Godzillas varying in size, so here is how big the monster is in Godzilla Minus One.

Godzilla Minus Zero is the latest film in the iconic monster movie franchise, and it's once again receiving some incredibly positive reviews, after it followed up the Oscar-winning Godzilla Minus One. The last film broke all kinds of box office records, with it being a smash hit and even becoming the largest domestic debut for a live-action Japanese film ever, and Minus Zero looks set to have a similar launch as well. Godzilla Minus Zero's success, combined with its beloved predecessor, has drawn a lot of eyes to the film, with many wondering how big Godzilla is in the latest film, especially when compared with other iterations of the character.

Godzilla is described as being 164 feet (50 meters) in Godzilla Minus One and its newly released sequel, Godzilla Minus Zero, setting the monster at a pretty fearsome size. While 164 feet is far from the biggest that Godzilla has been, this size makes him easily big enough to tower over cities and step on humans without even realizing it. Although some buildings are bigger than Godzilla in the film, the radioactive monster doesn't have much trouble leveling Japan thanks to his size. It's partially because of his size and power that he is recruited to help fight the dangerous King Ghidorah in Minus Zero.

While Godzilla is 164 feet for most of Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero, this isn't his only size. In fact, Godzilla actually changes size throughout the film. Before being mutated, Godzilla was still a pretty big monster, with him being about 50 feet tall. However, the 164-foot tall version is almost three times as big as it used to be, making Godzilla a horrifying threat.

Godzilla is comparatively small in Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero when looking at how big he is in other movies, but there is a reason why. Godzilla Minus One and its sequel hearken back to the original Godzilla movie from 1954, and in an attempt to link the two movies, the new movies actually made Godzilla the exact same height as he was in the 1954 original.

Godzilla Minus One and Godzilla Minus Zero sets its titular monster at 164 feet, causing many to wonder how that compares to Godzilla's size in other movies. As it turns out, Godzilla was also 164 feet (50 meters) in the original 1954 film, with Godzilla Minus One remaining consistent with the original movie. Godzilla stayed at this size through 1975's Terror of Mechagodzilla, with Godzilla growing to 262 feet tall for 1984's Return of Godzilla, only for him to grow to a whopping 328 feet in 1991's Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah, the biggest seen in a Japanese Godzilla until Shin Godzilla, in which he was 388 feet.

The first American Godzilla remake was released in 1998, with it portraying Godzilla as 229 feet tall. Godzilla grew even bigger in Legendary's Monsterverse, with him being 354 feet in 2014's Godzilla and growing to 394 feet for Godzilla: King of the Monsters and Godzilla vs. Kong. This makes the Monsterverse's iteration of Godzilla much bigger than the one seen in Godzilla Minus One, but that doesn't mean that they are scarier.

Although Godzilla is comparatively small in Godzilla Minus One and Minus Zero, the ending of the latter film sets the monster up to be even bigger in a potential sequel. As the film demonstrates, Godzilla has intense regenerative abilities, so much so that the heroes of the story claim with confidence that he would survive a nuclear blast. And, once again, it's for this very reason that they recruit Godzilla to fight against King Ghidorah.

Godzilla was injured when fighting the latter, so these regenerative abilities could end up causing Godzilla to grow even bigger upon his return in a sequel to Godzilla Minus Zero, meaning he could potentially grow to a size comparable with some other iterations of the character.

#3618. Legendary 31-Year-Old Space Western Officially Returns With New Release

While the Western genre is experiencing a bit of a comeback on-screen with the likes of Taylor Sheridan putting a modern twist on the genre, the same can't really be said for the space western. Plenty of sci-fi titles still share some loose, pulpy roots with classic Westerns, but there aren't many that evoke the same vibes as something like Firefly, Outland, or the classic anime Cowboy Bebop. This year did, however, see The Mandalorian and Grogu premiere in theaters and continue Jon Favreau's Star Wars spin-off series with a standalone cinematic adventure following the titular bounty hunter on a new mission. A storied anime Western is also about to make a return to the genre in a new form.

Per Anime News Network, Shueisha's Jump SQ. RISE magazine announced the return of Trigun in its autumn issue on Thursday, with a new novel penned by the legendary manga's creator Yasuhiro Nightow in collaboration with Trigun Stampede writer Takehiko Oxi. Titled Trigun Manuscript, it's slated to take place in the same world and continuity as Stampede and the most recent television anime, Trigun Stargaze, which premiered back in January. Stargaze was billed as the "final phase" of Stampede, closing out the reimagining of the story told in the source material and the Studio Madhouse series. While it's connected specifically to the 2023 anime, Nightow is also providing new art on both the cover and interior of the new release.

As far as the translation goes, it's described as "the long-awaited novelization," suggesting that it'll be a retelling of the events of Stampede and Stargaze. Shueisha hasn't announced an exact release date other than a general window of this winter. Further details are slated to be announced at a later date. Expectations are, however, that there will be some changes to Vash the Stampede's adventures now that the anime is wrapped up.

Produced by BEASTARS studio Orange, Trigun Stampede was the second adaptation of Nightow's 1995 manga, taking place in a far-flung future on a wasteland planet known as "No Man's Land." Vash the Stampede, also known as the Humanoid Typhoon, has earned himself a notorious reputation and a staggering bounty of $$60 billion for the accidental destruction he leaves in his wake. However, when rookie reporter Meryl Stryfe and her mentor Roberto De Niro run into the gun-slinging outlaw himself, they learn he's actually a pacifist who hates blood, using his skills to resolve conflicts rather than start them. Their chance encounter begins a wild adventure following the trail of Vash's despicable twin brother, Millions Knives, while avoiding the bounty hunters who inevitably come to claim the reward on Vash's head. Stargaze, meanwhile, picks up two and a half years later, after the Lost JuLai tragedy, with Vash now living in hiding under a different name until circumstances and Knives' genocidal plans force him back into action.

Trigun Manuscript releases this winter. Get a look at the cover and the official announcement above.
