#3598. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3597. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52 Emily Feingold Hired as EVP, Communications for The Walt Disney Company

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3596. Who Is Annatar? Sauron's Fair Form Explained

The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power introduces Sauron's fair form, Annatar. One of the most famous fictional villains of all time, he may be, but Sauron's physical appearance has always remained somewhat ambiguous. J.R.R. Tolkien describes Sauron in only the vaguest possible terms, and the popularized images of a towering warrior in black armor or a flaming eye atop Barad-dûr come mostly from Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movie trilogy.

Tolkien gets a little more descriptive about Sauron's appearance in Middle-earth's Second Age, which provides the setting for Amazon's The Rings of Power TV series. In canon, Sauron is licking his wounds following Morgoth's defeat. Upon finally reappearing, he takes the disguise of "Annatar," which Tolkien labels a "fair form" without ever really offering firm details. As Annatar plays a major role in The Rings of Power season 2, here's everything Middle-earth mythology reveals about Sauron's favorite face.

Though best known for his work in the field of warmongering, Sauron began as one of the Maiar - primordial, angel-adjacent, immortal spirits created as servants to the God of Tolkien's world, Eru Ilúvatar. Sauron would be corrupted by Melkor (later known as Morgoth), who was a higher-ranking spirit turned evil through greed, jealousy, and anger. All Maiar possess the ability to assume whatever physical form they desire, and many utilized this gift to mingle unseen among Elves and other Children of Ilúvatar. Sauron had other ideas, and exploited his shape-shifting to create a one-man Halloween party of guises.

During J.R.R. Tolkien's First Age, Sauron would change shape as a means of inspiring fear within his enemies. As the Second Age began, he perhaps realized the opposite would prove more effective, and returned to Middle-earth as "Annatar." Described by Tolkien as a "fair form," the author never offers a clear account of Annatar's handsome visage, but taking into consideration the kingdoms who accepted him as a valued friend, many have logically assumed Sauron's Annatar form was akin to an Elf or Númenórean.

The "Annatar" name was part of Sauron's deception too. The word means "Lord of Gifts" in the Quenya language of Elves - an allusion to how he promised knowledge, glory, wealth, and power to all those who heeded his great wisdom.

Sauron's first order of business as "Annatar" was deceiving the Elves, and duly made for Eregion, where the race's best smiths welcomed him. It's important to note that not all Elves trusted Annatar. The likes of Elrond, Gil-galad and Galadriel all deduced the newcomer's promises were too good to be true, and Annatar wouldn't venture near Lindon or Lothlórien as a result. Furthermore, none of the Elves - not even the suspicious ones - realized the deceitful Annatar was actually Sauron in disguise.

Sauron's purpose in Eregion was creating the Rings of Power. As a Maia, Sauron had served under Aulë, widely considered the god of blacksmiths and worshiped by Dwarves. Consequently, Sauron knew as much about craftsmanship as he did dark magic, and he put both to work while in Eregion. The Elves were keen to craft Rings of Power, and Sauron willingly offered his divine expertise on the matter. As recounted in The Fellowship of the Ring, Sauron betrayed his new friends by weaving a method of corrupting those who wore the Rings into their forging.

The sixteen Rings of Power later held by Dwarves and Men were directly influenced by Annatar. The Elves' three Rings were crafted by Celebrimbor personally, but still using Sauron's sinister method. Annatar then skulked back to Mordor and made his Ruling Ring, and only when Galadriel, Gil-galad and Círdan slipped on their three Rings did the Elves finally realize how badly they'd messed up.

Going into The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season 3, Sauron should be more or less done with his Annatar disguise. This season picks up after a five-year time jump, with the War of the Elves and Sauron well underway. For much of this time, Sauron's domination seems assured. However, he runs into a significant loss and is eventually taken to Númenor as Ar-Pharazôn's prisoner. In an effort to get on the corrupt king's good side, Sauron takes on a disguise once again. When this plays out on screen, we may get another look at Annatar.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

There's a cloud of ambiguity over which physical form Sauron adopted during his time on the island kingdom. Tolkien's writing heavily suggests the villain once again transformed into a "fair" shape, but never explicitly states whether Sauron recycled Annatar or picked something more befitting for his mortal hosts, and convincing arguments can be made both ways. Whatever he might've looked like, Sauron didn't stick with the "Annatar" moniker, since the people of Númenor already knew his true identity.

As he did with the Elves, Sauron charmed and manipulated those around him in Númenor. Instead of promising gifts and lore, however, he stoked the Númenóreans' existing anger toward the Valar, pushing them toward worshiping Morgoth instead. Sauron rose from a prisoner to Ar-Pharazôn's most valued advisor, ultimately convincing the King to embark on a foolhardy assault on Valinor.

Whether Sauron takes on his Annatar appearance in The Rings of Power season 3 or season 4, the fall of Númenor will, according to Tolkien, mean the definitive end of the Dark Lord's fair form. The massive wave that takes out the island kingdom takes out Sauron's physical body as well, leaving him a formless essence once again. Though he eventually reforms in Mordor, Sauron can never again take on any beautiful or seductive form. His evil must always show through his skin from that point onward. So, the time will come for Annatar to leave us forever.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3594. '9-1-1' Disappoints Fans Again With a Major Eddie Problem in Season 10

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 4.9-1-1 opened its tenth season with two especially compelling storylines: a volcanic eruption and a Buddie fight. While the volcano emergency was resolved in three episodes, it looked like Buck (Oliver Stark) and Eddie's (Ryan Guzman) argument would go on for longer. On the surface, they were arguing because Eddie had given Buck parental advice that he wasn't ready to hear. The deeper issue at play, though, seemed to be that, once again, Buck and Eddie were having conflict over the more ambiguous and undefined parts of their friendship that the two have not yet been ready to put to words.

The solution here seemed to be a simple one: Buck and Eddie needed to redefine the terms of their dynamic and their places in each other's lives, whatever that may look like, because what they'd had before was no longer enough. Instead, 9-1-1's latest episode, Season 10, Episode 4, "Imposter Syndrome," wraps this argument up way too quickly with an unearned off-screen resolution. While this is disappointing for multiple reasons, it's ultimately a symptom of 9-1-1's biggest problem at the moment: every time the show sets up a substantial storyline for Eddie, it ultimately sidelines him and fails to deliver.

Since returning from Texas at the end of Season 8, Eddie hasn't gotten a proper storyline of his own. Occasionally, 9-1-1 will lean into the fan-favorite pairing of Buck and Eddie, but every Buddie-centric storyline as of late always changes direction to become about Buck. When Buck pointed out last season that Eddie hadn't "even looked at a woman in a year" and pushed him to find someone, it looked like 9-1-1 might focus on Eddie and actually answer this question, potentially by giving him a storyline about his sexuality. Instead, the episode became all about Buck's hookups with a married couple. When the two had a fight and then got into a car accident in "Mother's Boy," the whole episode became about Eddie having to save Buck, and only Buck got to experience lingering effects from this trauma in the coming episodes.

There was no exploration of how the car accident affected Eddie, or the lingering impact that the racism and homophobia directed at him throughout that episode had on him. Even when Eddie got stabbed in the Season 9 finale, he recovered off-screen, and his pain was used to fuel Buck's storyline of choosing to foster Theo. Season 10's Buck and Eddie fight was set up to focus on Buck and Eddie's dynamic, but it could have also explored their own separate parenting issues. Instead, in "Imposter Syndrome," the storyline becomes all about Buck having problems with Theo (Lincoln and Theodore Sykes), because he still refuses to even try to parent him. Eddie is sidelined the whole episode, and he and Buck make up mostly off-screen, ending their argument with a brief conversation where Eddie has to comfort a self-deprecating Buck instead of having his own feelings acknowledged.

Eddie Diaz is one of the most captivating characters on television right now. He has a deeply compelling backstory, a fierce love for the people in his life, and an unshakable belief, on a fundamental level, that he doesn't deserve good things. There is so much for 9-1-1 to explore when it comes to Eddie's character, from his grief over recently losing Bobby and his abuela (Ana Mercedes), to his complicated relationship with religion, to why dating has never come easily to him. He hasn't had a proper storyline with Christopher (Gavin McHugh) since either of them moved back to Los Angeles, and the show hasn't given any focus to how Eddie felt about having stepped in for Chimney (Kenneth Choi) to primarily serve as a paramedic alongside Hen (Aisha Hinds) over a season ago.

The Buddie dynamic is certainly an important one, but Buck and Eddie have not been given the same treatment by the narrative, and every one of their shared storylines now always becomes about Buck. 9-1-1 needs to start focusing on Eddie's side of these storylines as well, but he also needs to get some deeper storylines of his own. Eddie already doesn't get enough to do, but when he does, 9-1-1 does not linger on him long enough to explore his feelings and the deeper implications that these storylines have had on him. In its tenth season, 9-1-1 is still underutilizing one of its best characters, and it needs to finally do right by him.

9-1-1 airs Thursdays at 8:00 P.M. EST on ABC.

#3593. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us onFacebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

JBL’s Live 780NC over-ear headphones are down to $139.95 from $249.95, a $110 discount that brings them to their lowest price ever, according to price trackers. At this price, you’re getting a feature-rich pair of wireless headphones with active noise cancellation, high-resolution audio support, and battery life that can last through several days of commuting or work sessions. They’re designed for people who like to wear headphones for hours at a time, too, with adjustable metal sliders and earcups that pivot to fit comfortably around your head. The earcups also fold flat to make them easier to pack, although the included soft pouch offers less protection in a bag than a hard case would.

Sound-wise, its 40mm drivers deliver a wide frequency response of 10Hz to 40kHz, while Bluetooth 6.0 support, LDAC, and LE Audio give you options for high-quality wireless listening with compatible devices. The catch is that the default tuning pushes the bass a little too hard (according to this PCMag review), so you may want to spend some time adjusting the sound through JBL’s app—which includes a 10-band equalizer, preset profiles, personalized sound settings, and virtual spatial audio, letting you tailor the listening experience to your preferences.

You also get Bluetooth multipoint for connecting two devices at once, plus a proximity sensor that pauses playback when you remove the headphones. Physical controls handle power, pairing, and volume, while a touch-sensitive surface lets you manage playback and call up your phone’s voice assistant. As for its battery life, JBL claims up to 80 hours of playback with active noise cancellation turned off, or up to 50 hours with ANC enabled. That should be plenty for long-haul flights, extended workdays, or several commutes between charges, although the noise cancellation itself isn’t quite as effective as what you’ll find on some higher-end competitors. The headphones also lack water and sweat resistance, so they’re not the best choice for workouts or rainy commutes.

#3591. ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases “Zi” in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

A Hong Kong violinist who’s losing her grip on reality, young Zi (Michelle Mao) is haunted by visions of her future self. The doctors at the local neurology center suspect that she might be suffering from the early symptoms of a brain tumor, but Zi — a being of pure cinema, cobbled together from the half-formed memories of films like “La Jetée” and “Cléo from 5 to 7” — will have to wait a long and lonely 24 hours for the test results to come back.  Related Stories ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Well, maybe not so lonely. Crying on one of the innumerable concrete steps that climb Lantau Island, Zi is consoled by a sweet American expat with a strangely familiar face (and an aggressively unnatural blonde wig). Her name is L, she’s a disillusioned former dancer played by the luminous Haley Lu Richardson, and she can’t help but reciprocate the inexplicable closeness that Zi feels towards her. Over the course of a single night together, these two lost souls will help to relocate each other in time — to resynchronize with the world around them, reconnect with the infinite potential of the present, and return themselves to the creative purpose that once anchored them to it.

Even if seen without a shred of context, it would be obvious to anyone that “Zi” was made by someone who is — or hopefully was — desperate to spark a realignment of his own. To steal himself away from regret and anxiety and tether his perspective back to the now. Shot without a script or a budget in the immediate aftermath of Kogonada’s ill-received “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” (the “After Yang” auteur’s studio debut, by all indications a soul-crushing experience for an artist whose two previous features retained the delicate grace of the video essays that he used to make), this searching and unformed wisp of an experiment hardly represents the first time that an ascendent director has scaled down after a misstep, but “Zi” takes the notion of “one for me” to much greater and more galvanizing extremes than usual.

This isn’t just a filmmaker trying to get back on track, it’s a filmmaker desperately, nakedly searching for a way to fall back in love with filmmaking itself. A way to prove that it might still love him back. (Kogonada described the project to IndieWire as “A retreat, as well as a pursuit.”)

While the prospect of watching Kogonada do that will naturally be of greater interest to those who have watched him get to this point, this movie’s palpably improvised nature — its stolen shots and recursive shape lend the impression of someone trying to cut their ultra-evocative vacation footage into a coherent narrative — would force anyone to wonder about the meta-textual aspects of its creation. “You feel like your sole purpose in life is something, and it doesn’t choose you back,” L sputters out at one point. “What do you do with that? I had to get away from it all. That’s why I came here. Wandering.”

Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed.

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present.

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals.

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes.

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3590. The Bose Premium Smart Ultra Soundbar Is Now Cheaper Than It Was During Prime Day

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3589. Before Solo Leveling Returns, Another Anime Is Stealing Its Thunder

The demand for Solo Leveling is absurdly high as 2026 comes to a close. Hype has gone up considerably even for its follow-up story, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok as it confirmed season 3 was on the way, and the upcoming Solo Leveling: Beyond the System film is certainly going to garner more attention than the compilation film ahead of season 2. But for those who appreciate its action and LitRPG and progression fantasy elements while seeking something arguably far less serious, yet extremely fun and still quite competently animated, fall 2026 has had one truly worthwhile alternative: Overgeared.

Produced by J.C.Staff, Overgeared stands as a reminder of the studio's potential for well-received anime with the right staff attached. It's produced an interesting arc so far, starring a character who may not be wholly likable, yet entirely too compelling and entertaining all the same in Shin Youngwoo, or "Grid" as his online handle in the fictional VRMMORPG "SATISFY". While it's had some striking animated sequences including spectacular, show-stopping attacks, this anime taps into the entertaining, relatable world of the MMO crafting grind, the prospect of monetizing success in the game to generate real cash, and working one's way out of debt. It's also got its fair share of surprises for fans of the dub.

For fans of Solo Leveling who are perhaps dismayed by Sung Jinwoo's gradual deteriorated sense of emotional vulnerability, Grid is quite the opposite. Rather than being the weakest hunter like Jinwoo's earliest days, Grid's daily life as Youngwoo is one constantly saddled with debt, living with his family as a Not in Education, Employment, or Training adult, or NEET. But in SATISFY, people can become celebrities and grow rich off major accomplishments, and in Youngwoo's case, after encountering a class change turning him into Pagma's Successor, he's able to craft drastically better equipment, auctioning or outright contracting his work to NPCs with deep pockets.

It sets up a different yet entirely authentic alternative path for Grid to be a Legendary-level smith, capable of crafting Epic, Unique, or Legendary equipment, placing him handily above anybody else. Rather than replicating Jinwoo's power fantasy path, this feels almost more like an escape from debt and poverty, especially as the latest episodes soon turn the tables, Grid overcoming his debt while suddenly having to dig his family out of debt. But make no mistake: Grid isn't suddenly a noble character overnight after finally getting a taste of success, and that's ok.

Fans will find Grid harder to like in the strictest sense, as his instincts for self-preservation are hard to overlook. But for manhwa readers familiar with this particular type of character, much like Lloyd Frontera, Grid is hilariously over-the-top in everything he does. He's wildly entertaining, and even his compounded flaws make for more a more engaging personality than Jinwoo could ever manage. Overgeared has already introduced numerous high-stakes in-game quests for Grid to overcome, a growing supporting cast including Huroi, whose own unique in-game situation puts him in Grid's orbit, all of which make for fun alternatives to Solo Leveling characters like Jinho and more. But one Overgeared experience is entirely unique compared to Solo Leveling's.

Ricco Fajardo is a treat as Grid in Overgeared's English dub, but not just for giving it 110% in every scene. Much like Aleks Le as Jinwoo, Fajardo likes to have a bit of fun in the ADR process, but in the latter's case, they keep even his most unhinged recordings as they still stick to the script and spirit of the story. So English dub Grid might make the occasional reference to memes like "Democracy Manifest" featuring Jack Karlson, little offhand comments, or even "your mom" jokes, with fans eagerly compiling Overgeared's dubbed absurdity. It feels at times more like TFS Abridged production, which should absolutely be considered a compliment, even if the parody energy might undermine its authenticity at times.

Solo Leveling may be a great story, but it is nothing compared to its sequel manga, Solo Leveling: Ragnarok, and fans are not ready for it.

The result isn't a wholly reinvented, legendary dub on the level of Ghost Stories presenting practically a new story, but rather, just a fun hidden treat for fans who prefer dubs over subs. With six episodes released, and six more on the way, subbed fans equally get the opportunity to enjoy Grid's adventures as he finally gets to embark on major quests as Pagma's Successor, while dub fans get access to a production not often seen in the saturated anime landscape. Solo Leveling isn't going anywhere just yet, and Overgeared is just the sort of high-energy palate cleanser to keep fans entertained going into 2027.

#3588. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying

No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

This grounding process is especially important, and especially challenging, when things that should be on the ground take to the air as a part of Ghidorah’s gravity beam. Inoue did an initial pass of the sound effect for the beam that allows Ghidorah to throw whole houses up in the air high enough for our favorite eternally tormented, former Kamikaze pilot Kôichi Skikishima (Ryûnosuke Kamiki) to fly past them. But it wasn’t quite right.

“So I went back into the Foley studio, and I wanted to capture that feeling of something being lifted and rising. I took this very small speaker, and I placed it right next to a bunch of different objects — a sheet of metal or some wood or a water tank — to capture a sound that almost felt distorted,” Inoue said.

That distortion, bounced off different types of objects, captured the sensation Inoue was after: the sonic equivalent of your stomach lifting into your mouth.

“Oftentimes in sound design, when you layer too many sounds or put too much processing on it, it starts to ruin the original material or the original sound that you’ve captured. So this distortion became a very strong foundation. I didn’t add too much post-processing on it,” Inoue said.

What she did do was hand it over to Takeuchi to create the sense of whole blocks caught up in Ghidorah’s gravity beam and preserve the dialogue and add background dialogue, so that we’re always afraid for the human beings in danger during Ghidorah’s rampages.

When Shikishima first flies through Ghidorah’s gravity beam, the sound team really wanted to lean into the character’s emotional response to something that’s mindbendingly horrible. “I added a Doppler effect — so like when an ambulance or a police car drives by and the sound shifts slightly — [to give] the sensation that you’re passing through,” Takeuchi told IndieWire.

It’s that shifting of sound, more than any one particular sound, that adds a scale to the horror beyond what Shikishima or what we can see. “We wanted to be very mindful of the balance and what it was doing and what it was supposed to do for each scene,” Takeuchi said.

“What we were trying to do is take sounds that you would hear in nature and then design and add to it in almost like an extension type of way, and that’s how we make the Kaiju as well as the gravity beam feel more real,” Inoue added.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3587. Apple CEO John Ternus criticized for ‘scripted’ approach to first earnings call

Investors didn’t seem overly happy about yesterday’s Apple earnings call despite the record results. That likely reflects the company’s cautious take on margins in the current quarter, but some have also criticized what they describe as a very “scripted” approach by new CEO John Ternus.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

#3586. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3585. 10 Greatest Sam Rockwell Movies, Ranked

With a career spanning over 30 years, Sam Rockwell has established himself as an actor who can disappear into any role. The size of the part never matters, because Rockwell makes five minutes on screen so memorable that it feels like he's the lead star of the movie.

Possessing an effortless charm that adds layers to his dramatic roles and likability to his comedic turns, Rockwell is the actor who elevates any part that he chooses to play. Whether it was as an out-of-control convict in The Green Mile, or as the President of the United States in Vice, Rockwell steals every scene he's in. Ahead of his latest films, Wild Horse Nine and Ray Gunn, the following films showcase Rockwell's skills and serve as a reminder that he's one of the most exciting actors working today.

In The Best of Enemies, Rockwell plays C.P. Ellis, the president of the Ku Klux Klan in 1970s Durham, North Carolina. When the local black school burns down, community organizer Ann Atwater (Taraji P. Henson) and C.P. are forced to work together to establish a peaceful transition into desegregation. Although the two first find it impossible to coexist, they begin to connect, leading to C.P. questioning his values.

Rockwell is no stranger to playing characters with deplorable beliefs, but at least in The Best of Enemies his character is allowed a redemptive journey. Based on the book The Best of Enemies: Race and Redemption in the New South by Osha Gray Davidson, the film sheds light on a lesser-known true story about the lessons learned through desegregation. The Best of Enemies will hit familiar notes of other like-minded movies, but feels fresh based on the strength of the performances from Rockwell and Henson, who work off of one another's energy in both moments of anger and understanding.

Rockwell took the highest office when he appeared as President George W. Bush in the Adam McKay satire, Vice. Following the life and controversies of former Vice President Dick Cheney, (Christian Bale) Vice is a comedy of the darkest nature with biting political commentary. The biographical depiction of Cheney shows his rise to power within the White House, made possible by Bush's invitation to be his running mate.

Rockwell might not be the obvious choice to play President Bush, but with the aid of only a little makeup, he transforms into the former Commander in Chief. The film's core focus is on former Vice President Cheney, but that didn't prevent Rockwell from catching critics' attention with his affable portrayal of Bush. Vice would go on to receive multiple Academy Award nominations, including a Best Supporting Actor nod for Rockwell.

Earlier in his career, Rockwell played a part in another controversial politician's career in the Ron Howard-directed Frost/Nixon. The film, an adaptation of the stage play of the same name by Peter Morgan, tells the story of a series of taped one-on-one interviews between British journalist David Frost (Michael Sheen) and disgraced president Richard Nixon (Frank Langella).

While the film is primarily carried on the strength of Langella and Sheen's performances in their title roles, Rockwell received strong critical praise for his supporting performance as the strong-willed Jim Reston Jr. As an investigator who assists Frost in his preparation for the interviews, Rockwell brings a ferocious intensity as a professor with passionate feelings about Nixon's administration and the crimes he feels the former President wasn't held accountable for. Frost/Nixon gave Rockwell a chance to shine in a large production, and he didn't waste the opportunity.

The offbeat satirical comedy Jojo Rabbit follows a 10-year-old boy, Johannes "Jojo" Betzler (Roman Griffin Davis), who is a loyal member of a Hitler Youth group during the collapse of the Nazi forces. The lonely Jojo spends his time playing with his imaginary friend Hitler (Taika Waititi) and his mother Rosie (Scarlett Johansson), who harbors secret resentment toward the Nazi party. As Jojo tries to prove himself to the local armed forces, he discovers Rosie is hiding a young woman, Elsa (Thomasin McKenzie), from the Nazis.

Rockwell is incredibly funny as the apathetic leader of the Nazi youth, Captain Klenzendorf. Rockwell's embodiment of a soldier disillusioned with both the war and the side he's fighting on is somehow as nuanced in its sorrow as it is broad in its comedy. Klenzendorf isn't in much of Jojo Rabbit, but as is usually the case with Rockwell, the time he's on-screen is electric. His affection for Jojo leads to a few emotionally heartbreaking scenes as Klenzendorf makes his last moments ones to protect his young friend.

One of Rockwell's earliest roles that drew acclaim was his performance in the indie drama Lawn Dogs. The gated community of Camelot Gardens may look pristine from the outside, but the disaffected families that live in its suburban grounds are far from happy. When a member of the community, ten-year-old Devon (Mischa Barton), befriends a groundskeeper, Trent (Rockwell), their innocent friendship sends the wrong message to the wrong people.

Lawn Dogs gave Rockwell one of his first larger roles, and he delivers an understated performance in his interactions with the persistent attempts at friendship by the young Devon. The film approaches scenes within Camelot Gardens in a dreamlike presentation that carries an undertone of menace for every interaction Devon has. The surreal structure of Lawn Dogs might not be for everyone, but fans of Rockwell who haven't seen it should make the time.

A coming-of-age story gives Rockwell one of his most charming roles in the dramedy The Way, Way Back. The film follows Duncan (Liam James), a 14-year-old boy who is forced into a summer vacation with his mother Pam (Toni Collette) and her volatile boyfriend Trent (Steve Carell). With his mother wrapped up in her relationship, Duncan explores their vacation spot and meets Owen (Rockwell), a man who works at the local water park. The two develop a bond, and Owen offers him a summer job to help at the park.

Rockwell channels his best Bill Murray in Meatballs while providing mentorship to a boy he can tell needs a friend. Rockwell's relaxed charisma is on full display for every scene in The Way, Way Back, and his natural comic timing makes it surprising that he didn't do more traditional comedies. Everyone in the cast does a great job in this rewatchable gem, but Rockwell will be the reason viewers come back to The Way, Way Back for a second or third watch.

One of the movies Rockwell fans commonly point to as their favorite is the slow-burn sci-fi drama Moon. Sam Bell (Rockwell) is close to finishing up his three-year contract as the sole operator of a space station, but he begins to suspect his situation may be more dire than he assumed. As Sam pulls on the thread of his own existence, he finds that what he knew to be the truth was all an elaborate lie.

Without including any spoilers for Moon, the film is a wholly original mystery that continues to develop with satisfying reveals. A movie starring one person can be daunting to watch, but Rockwell is compelling throughout the runtime, and the film doesn't lag thanks to his performance. Even if viewers guess some of the plot twists in advance, it doesn’t take away from Sam’s emotional fallout from the discoveries.

The lonely last stop before execution is the setting for the supernatural drama The Green Mile. Paul Edgecomb (Tom Hanks) oversees the normally mundane death row in a 1930s prison, but that all changes with the arrival of a kind and gentle inmate named John Coffey (Michael Clarke Duncan). Coffey was convicted of the brutal murder of two young girls, but the crime doesn’t match the sweet-natured disposition of the man awaiting execution. As Paul learns the truth behind the crimes, he'll find his life forever changed.

Even though he has a small role in The Green Mile, Rockwell commands the screen for every second as the wild and feral prisoner William "Wild Bill" Wharton. Wild Bill is the polar opposite of Coffey, continually disruptive and violent without any remorse for the crimes that landed him on death row. Even though Rockwell exudes charm naturally, he brings none to one of his most chaotic characters.

An underrated classic that doesn't get the attention it deserves, Confessions of a Dangerous Mind was an early opportunity to show what Rockwell looked like as a leading man. Based on the autobiography of the same name, Confessions of a Dangerous Mind tells the life story of game show producer Chuck Barris (Rockwell). According to Barris, he allegedly worked as a spy and government assassin while creating some of television's most popular shows, like The Dating Game and The Newlywed Game.

The part of Chuck Barris made its way around Hollywood with multiple names attached, but it was when George Clooney took over as director that he lobbied for Rockwell to play the eccentric producer. Although the studio was skeptical of casting the then-unknown Rockwell, he would eventually secure the part of Barris and receive critical acclaim for his dynamic and energetic portrayal. This is an absolute must-watch for any fans of Rockwell.

A grieving mother will not be ignored in the award-winning drama, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri. The film follows Mildred Hayes (Frances McDormand), a frustrated and heartbroken mother to a daughter who was raped and murdered by an unknown assailant. Fed up with the ineptitude of the local police, Mildred posts messages about her daughter's case on billboards near town to demand attention. As the presence of the billboards brings negative attention to her, she relentlessly pursues the truth.

As one of the police officers opposing Mildred's billboard, Jason Dixon is one of Rockwell's crowning achievements. As the movie goes on, the boorish exterior of Dixon is continually pulled away in small pieces, revealing a man who is struggling to hide his own pain and disappointment until he has no choice but to look within. Rockwell's role as the violent and stubborn Officer Dixon would win him his first and only (so far) Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor.

A mother personally challenges the local authorities to solve her daughter's murder when they fail to catch the culprit.

#3584. The Cat In The Hat Sets Up A Sequel That Could Rival The Minions Franchise

There's a brand-new Cat in the Hat in town with 2026's animated movie The Cat in the Hat, and not only has this film just given this fan-favorite character another go on the big screen, but also, it's teased that so much more could be coming. The Cat in the Hat as a broader story hasn't had the easiest time. In fact, 2003's The Cat in the Hat was heavily criticized, and it remains, unfortunately, an example of what not to do when bringing a beloved children's story to life in live-action.

The new animated movie is a massive improvement, although reviews of The Cat in the Hat still suggest some issues, from a plot that is attempting to do a bit too much and ultimately becomes unwieldy, especially towards the end, to villains whose motivations make no sense and more. Currently, The Cat in the Hat's Rotten Tomatoes score reflects similar sentiments, with the audience score not yet revealed but the critic score sitting at a bleak 46%. Yet, that only makes one blink-and-you-miss-it moment in the movie all the more interesting.

Specifically, while no sequels to The Cat in the Hat have been announced yet, and that possibility may very well still depend upon the reception of the movie (which isn't looking great, based on current scores), one line from The Cat in the Hat has suggested that a sequel is already underway—or, at the very least, being seriously considered—and it could actually rival the biggest animated movie franchise of all time, if it's done correctly.

While the main narrative of The Cat in the Hat is focused on the titular Cat, along with siblings Gabby and Sebastian, the former of whom gets considerably more screen time, there are numerous characters in this movie, many of them a match for Dr. Seuss's fantastical, whimsical style. That includes a group of creatures almost as iconic as the Cat in the Hat himself: the Things. Those loosely familiar with Dr. Seuss are probably aware of Thing 1 and Thing 2, but The Cat in the Hat introduces a whole group of Things, all with unique styles and personalities.

If that concept sounds vaguely familiar, that's because it should; no doubt intentionally, this group of goofy, slap-stick humor-filled yet adorable little creatures feels like a direct competitor to the Minions. What's more, The Cat in the Hat has directly teased the possibility of the Things returning in their own standalone movie, as, at one point, the Cat is trying to get them back in their box and tells them not to worry because they will get their own movie soon. Sure, that could just be played for a laugh, but it actually seems like a serious prospect.

And, notably, it's one that could compete with the biggest franchise out there. After debuting in Despicable Me, and continuing to appear in those sequels, the Minions have managed to get their own run of movies, with the most recent, Minions & Monsters, hitting theaters just this year. When taking the entire franchise into account, including the Despicable Me movies and Minions movies, this is the highest-grossing animated movie franchise of all time, by a surprisingly wide margin. Now, the question just remains whether a Dr. Seuss franchise could really give the Minions a run for their money.

The current reception of The Cat in the Hat sadly doesn't seem to be laying the groundwork for a massive franchise the likes of which could compete with the formidable Minions. Yet, not all hope is lost. For one, audience scores haven't really begun rolling in yet, and those could be a key determining factor, especially in the eyes of the studio. In fact, it feels more likely than not that the Things will be the standout for audiences, particularly young audiences, and that might mean green lighting a Things movie, at which point, this franchise has a real chance.

Found an error? Send it info@screenrant.com so it can be corrected.

There's also, honestly, no good reason why there couldn't be an enormously successful Dr. Seuss cinematic universe if that's what the powers that be wanted to do. These characters and stories have obviously had staying power, and there is so much opportunity to bridge the characters and stories together in a way that actually builds out a franchise. Now, it's just a waiting game to see whether audiences like The Cat in the Hat and, if so, whether that's enough to get the ball fully rolling with a Things movie.
